newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac's record on presidential campaign promises.
newsitem.headline: Chirac's record on presidential campaign promises.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac urged French voters in a television appeal on Tuesday not to put at risk the achievements of his two years in office by voting for a return to socialism.
Chirac was elected in May 1995 on a host of campaign promises. Here is an account of what happened to them.
UNEMPLOYMENT - Chirac promised to put fighting unemployment at the top of his list of priorities and heal what he called "the social fracture".

"Above all, I will do everything in my power to restore France's social cohesion and renew the Republican pact with the French people. Employment will be my constant concern," he said in his inaugural address on May 17, 1995.
In October 1995, he decreed two years of budget austerity in a turnabout making spending cuts the "priority of priorities".

Unemployment has risen from 11.5 percent of the workforce at the time of his election to a record 12.8 percent. More than 3.1 million people are eligible for unemployment benefit and the total number without work is closer to four million when people on minimum state assistance are counted.
The government says it has virtually halted the increase in the jobless total and that the economy is now creating more jobs than it is losing, but the workforce is growing still faster.
A law introduced last year granting private sector firms relief from heavy social security charges if they shorten the work week to save jobs has slowed redundancies, officials say.
EUROPE - After briefly toying with the idea of another referendum on European economic and monetary union during the 1995 campaign, Chirac promised to lead France into a single European currency.
A survey for the weekly Le Nouvel Economiste last month showed that two thirds of voters believed he had kept this promise, the only commitment he was found to have honoured.
TAX CUTS - Chirac promised that he would lower taxes quickly if elected, using the election slogan "too much tax kills tax".
Under his government, the tax burden reached a record 45.7 percent last year.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe immediately increased Value Added Tax by two points to 20.6 percent and introduced a new tax in 1995 to pay off debts accumulated by the state welfare system.
In September 1996, the government announced a five-year plan to cut income tax by 75 billion francs (then $13 billion) with 25 billion in 1997.
But an increase in a savings levy to help fund the welfare system reduced net tax cuts to 18 billion francs. With increases in local authority taxes, few voters felt better off.
PUBLIC SECTOR - Chirac promised to boost public sector salaries and pledged that health care would not be rationed or subjected to spending limits.

Reforms were launched in late 1995 to streamline public health care, retirement and family benefits and end chronic social security deficits by setting annual limits on the increase in welfare spending.

The proposals, including making civil servants work longer for a full pension, sparked a crippling 24-day transport strike. Juppe dropped the later-retirement plan but stuck to the core of his health spending curbs. ($ = 5.715 French Francs)
